ip.name: Public IP Address
ip.whatChecked: Your Public IP address, Internet Service Provider (ISP), and Autonomous System Number (ASN).
ip.whyAccess: Websites need your IP address to send web page data back to your device; without it, internet routing is physically impossible.
ip.privacyImpact: An IP acts as a semi-permanent tracking number that logs your approximate coordinates and correlates all network requests back to your home router.
ip.realWorldExample: Copyright holders monitor IP address lists on BitTorrent networks to identify users downloading media and issue copyright strikes.
ip.protection: Use a Virtual Private Network (VPN) or the Tor browser to route traffic through an encrypted tunnel, masking your real residential IP.
ip.learnMore: An IP (Internet Protocol) address functions like a return address on an envelope. Using proxies swaps this address for another.

browser.name: Browser User-Agent
browser.whatChecked: The User-Agent header string which lists your browser brand, rendering engine version, and system languages.
browser.whyAccess: Websites query the User-Agent header to deliver custom styled pages optimized for your specific browser software (e.g. mobile vs. desktop styling).
browser.privacyImpact: The precise version numbers of your browser and its extensions narrow down your identity, creating a unique signature.
browser.realWorldExample: Websites track browser version distributions to serve targeted exploits or notice if a browser uses obsolete, vulnerable releases.
browser.protection: Enable generic browser headers overrides or use privacy browsers (such as Firefox or Brave) that mask details in standard requests.
browser.learnMore: User-Agents help developers support legacy systems, but advertising networks abuse them to construct tracking profiles.

os.name: Operating System
os.whatChecked: Your system software profile (e.g., Windows 11, macOS Sequoia, Linux Kernel) and CPU architecture.
os.whyAccess: Websites inspect your OS to download correct binary file installers (e.g. suggesting .exe for Windows and .dmg for macOS) and match performance rendering engines.
os.privacyImpact: Exposes your device brand and sub-version, which trackers use to group your device with other similar entities in their databases.
os.realWorldExample: Ad systems noticed that users browsing from macOS devices statistically buy higher-priced items, prompting sites to adjust search rankings.
os.protection: Block native hardware query APIs and avoid installing system-specific customization packages that report custom device parameters.
os.learnMore: Your operating system dictates font rendering styles, screen layouts, and network protocols, which websites scan on load.

location.name: Physical Geolocation
location.whatChecked: The discrepancy between your IP-based geolocation (from local ISP databases) and your device's raw GPS sensor coordinates.
location.whyAccess: IP location is checked automatically based on your network route. GPS location requests your browser's sensor permission to provide high-accuracy mapping.
location.privacyImpact: While IP coordinates resolve to a city or ISP node (often 5-15 miles away), GPS location can pinpoint your exact street address within meters.
location.realWorldExample: Local weather apps and food delivery sites require precise GPS access to identify your physical residence for dispatching services.
location.protection: Deny browser GPS permissions to untrusted sites and toggle location services off on your system settings.
location.learnMore: IP location maps are based on static IP registration records, whereas browser GPS query hardware satellites and nearby Wi-Fi router coordinates.

webrtc.name: WebRTC Local IP Leak
webrtc.whatChecked: Local network LAN IPs (e.g. 192.168.1.x) exposed via ICE candidate protocol handshakes.
webrtc.whyAccess: WebRTC requires direct peer-to-peer data channels for lag-free video chats and audio calling, bypasses intermediate servers.
webrtc.privacyImpact: Unmasks your real internal home IP address even when your external public IP is securely wrapped inside a VPN tunnel.
webrtc.realWorldExample: Tracking engines run hidden WebRTC scripts to detect users employing cheap proxies, matching their real local subnet values.
webrtc.protection: Install a WebRTC block extension or set 'media.peerconnection.enabled' to false in Firefox advanced configuration menus.
webrtc.learnMore: WebRTC requests ICE candidates directly from the OS routing table. Since STUN queries are local, standard browser extensions fail to intercept them.

dnsleak.name: DNS Tunnel Leak
dnsleak.whatChecked: The subnets of your active Domain Name System (DNS) resolver servers compared to your public IP range.
dnsleak.whyAccess: To load website domains, your computer queries DNS servers to translate text addresses (like google.com) to numeric IP coordinates.
dnsleak.privacyImpact: If your DNS queries route outside your encrypted VPN tunnel, your local ISP can log and monitor every single website domain you visit.
dnsleak.realWorldExample: In countries with active censorship, ISPs intercept leaking DNS lookups to block access to specific domain names or catalog user activity logs.
dnsleak.protection: Choose VPN clients with built-in DNS leak block protections and configure secure DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) inside browser properties.
dnsleak.learnMore: A DNS leak occurs when your operating system defaults to using your ISP's automatic DNS server instead of the secure DNS server provided by the VPN.

canvas.name: HTML5 Canvas Fingerprint
canvas.whatChecked: Graphic rendering differences in shapes, gradients, and font anti-aliasing weights.
canvas.whyAccess: The Canvas API is a standard HTML5 feature used by developers to render dynamic games, images, and interactive graphics locally.
canvas.privacyImpact: Creates a permanent, cookieless hardware tracking token. Since rendering is tied to your GPU driver, the generated text hash is highly unique.
canvas.realWorldExample: Commercial tracker scripts embed invisible 1x1 canvas drawing traps to recognize individual users across private incognito sessions.
canvas.protection: Use extensions that inject random pixel noise into canvas outputs to invalidate the consistency of the tracking hash.
canvas.learnMore: Canvas fingerprinting exploits the fact that no two graphics card drivers draw curves and letters with identical sub-pixel weights.

audio.name: Web Audio Fingerprint
audio.whatChecked: Mathematical sound wave frequency synthesis variance in your browser's audio processing pipeline.
audio.whyAccess: The Web Audio API allows pages to generate, synthesize, and control sound effects in games or complex web-based audio applications.
audio.privacyImpact: Determines a unique hardware audio profile that persists across browser sessions and operates independently of cookies.
audio.realWorldExample: Ad brokers cross-reference canvas and audio hashes to reconstruct cross-domain profiles of anonymous visitors.
audio.protection: Block or restrict audio synthesis node executions, or use browsers that automatically pad sound synthesis calculations with noise.
audio.learnMore: Audio fingerprinting measures mathematical differences in sound processing algorithms, which vary based on your system sound card chip.

webgl.name: WebGL GPU Fingerprint
webgl.whatChecked: Unmasked WebGL graphic vendor, GPU renderer specifications, and WebGL drawing buffer rendering hashes.
webgl.whyAccess: WebGL is needed to render high-performance interactive 3D graphics (like Google Earth or web games) directly in your browser.
webgl.privacyImpact: Exposes your exact graphics card model (e.g. NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3070, Apple M2 GPU), dramatically narrowing down your device anonymity.
webgl.realWorldExample: Game platforms scan your GPU details to automatically configure optimal graphical settings or verify device capability indexes.
webgl.protection: Disable WebGL inside browser configs (webgl.disabled in Firefox) or use privacy extensions that block GPU info access.
webgl.learnMore: Trackers combine WebGL details with screen measurements to create a comprehensive device profile that identifies your hardware configuration.

vpnOrTor.name: Network Anonymizer Route
vpnOrTor.whatChecked: Whether your IP address belongs to standard residential ranges, cloud hosting datacenters, or Tor exit relays.
vpnOrTor.whyAccess: Websites inspect your connection route to verify that traffic originates from a real human device rather than an automated server bot.
vpnOrTor.privacyImpact: Datacenter IPs and Tor relays are heavily monitored. Trackers block or flag these connections, forcing CAPTCHAs or denying service.
vpnOrTor.realWorldExample: Streaming providers check connection ranges against database registries to block users attempting to bypass geographic licensing limitations.
vpnOrTor.protection: Use premium VPN providers that offer residential IP proxies, or configure bridges to mask Tor exit traffic.
vpnOrTor.learnMore: Datacenter ranges belong to hosting companies (AWS, GCP). Residential ranges belong to home connections (Comcast, AT&T), which sites trust more.

capabilities.name: Local Storage & Cookies
capabilities.whatChecked: Browser capabilities including Cookie support, LocalStorage, SessionStorage, IndexedDB, and Service Workers.
capabilities.whyAccess: Cookies and LocalStorage are standard features used to save your website preferences, login sessions, and shopping cart items.
capabilities.privacyImpact: When misused, persistent storage acts as tracking cookies. Trackers store long-term tracking IDs that identify your device across visits.
capabilities.realWorldExample: Shopping sites save persistent tracking tokens in your LocalStorage to show ads for items you viewed, even after you clear cookies.
capabilities.protection: Configure your browser to block third-party cookies and clear all site storage automatically upon closing browser windows.
capabilities.learnMore: Standard cookies are limited in size (4KB), whereas LocalStorage allows sites to save up to 5MB of persistent data on your computer.

security.name: Security Configuration
security.whatChecked: HTTPS connection status, Secure Context parameters, mixed-content filters, and Referrer headers leakage.
security.whyAccess: HTTPS ensures your traffic is encrypted. Secure Context limits powerful APIs to safe connections. Referrer tells sites where you navigated from.
security.privacyImpact: Unencrypted connections allow local networks to intercept passwords. Leaked referrers expose your exact navigation history.
security.realWorldExample: A user navigating from a private portal to a public store leaks their user account ID in the Referrer URL path.
security.protection: Force HTTPS-Only mode in browser settings and configure strict Referrer policies (such as 'no-referrer' or 'same-origin').
security.learnMore: HTTPS establishes a secure tunnel using TLS encryption. Secure Contexts prevent dangerous features (like camera access) on insecure HTTP pages.
